newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Export tax is highlight of week in Brazil Congress.
newsitem.headline: Export tax is highlight of week in Brazil Congress.

text.p: As the Congress enters what could be the last week of voting before the onset of municipal elections, Brazil's government is urging quick action on tax relief for exporters and manufacturers.
Planning Minister Antonio Kandir will go to the Senate on Tuesday to urge senators to give the bill priority treatment in the upper house, a ministry spokeswoman said.

The bill would reduce the scope of a tax, known as ICMS, which is levied by state governments. The proposed law would exempt this tax from being applied to exports as well as capital goods, energy and other inputs used by manufacturers.
This week could well be the last in which the Congress votes before the first round of municipal elections Oct. 3.
Should the ICMS bill be given priority treatment on Tuesday, the Senate would have 48 hours to vote on the measure.

Kandir's spokeswoman said the minister was concerned at reports that exports were building up in ports across the country as traders await final approval of the bill which has already cleared the lower house.

Also in the Senate, a bill authorizing the Central Bank to buy back Brady bonds and to swap them for sovereign debt was due to be put to a vote in a committee on Tuesday. If approved, the bill would then be put to a final vote on floor of the Senate.
The government was expected to seek priority treatment in the Chamber of Deputies for a bill spelling out the small print of the check tax to fund the health service.

The tax, which has been approved in principle by the lower house, would levy a 0.2 percent charge on financial transactions over a year. Pensioners and the poor are expected to be exempted by the regulatory legislation.
Another bill which may be given priority treatment this week in the Chamber of Deputies would slash taxes paid by small companies.

The government's economic team is opposed to the bill, which it says could cost up to $4 billion in lost revenues, and government leaders in the lower house are expected to attempt to block its progress.
A Chamber of Deputies committee was scheduled to vote Tuesday on a proposed parliamentary inquiry into PROER, a program to assist mergers and acquisitions in the private banking sector.
However, the government has managed to avoid a vote on the proposed parliamentary inquiry four times in the last month.
